images.filename: Sultan of Delhi Flag according to the Catalan Atlas (1375).png
images.caption:
Flag of the Sultanate of Delhi according to the Catalan Atlas (1375). The flag is grey with a black band in the Catalan Atlas (attached image), not green with a black band as previously uploaded. The actual grey and black color appears clearly in the primary source (and the Catalan Atlas has plenty of green otherwise, so the grey cannot be a result of color fading), and this interpretation is confirmed by academic sources:
REFERENCE: "....that helps to identify yet another curious flag found in northern India – a brown or originally sliver flag with a vertical black line – as the flag of the Delhi Sultanate (602-962/1206-1555)." in (2010). "On the Timurid flag". Beiträge zur islamischen Kunst und Archäologie 2: 148.
WARNING: This is primary source image, the actual flag is otherwise unknown. The main source pointing to this design is the Catalan Atlas, which as a historical primary source. This image should not be added to articles without clearly attributing its primary source origin, and secondary sources are additionally desired if available (such as the one above).  Note that FOTW (where most of those flags on Commons are adapted from) is based on user contributions like Wikipedia, and hence not authoritative.

images.filename: Aamkhas palace or Diwan-e-Aam inside Daulatabad Fort alias Deogiri Fort, Daulatabad, Maharashtra, India 01.jpg
images.caption:
Aamkhas palace or Diwan-e-Aam inside Daulatabad Fort alias Deogiri Fort, Daulatabad, Maharashtra, India,
The Aamkhas palace or Diwan-e-Aam is a mansion which is  originally an entrance to another palace complex and royal Hammam, but later this entrance was closed and converted into a palace. This palace had a central hall with high flat roof flanked by double storeyed cells and stairs leading to upper story. The ceiling of the roof is decorated with diamond cut stucco moldings. Standing on a high raised platform, this palace gives a commanding view to the nearby area. In front of the palace is an extensive courtyard adopted for environmental and architectural harmony.

This palace now houses the fort museum studded with rich collection of art objects, such as sculptures mostly recovered from the excavations of this fort. The open air gallery in front of this palace exhibits a number of sculptures and architectural members, utensils of different sizes, coins, beads of semi precious stones, arms and Armory etc.

images.filename: Andheri or Dark Passage located inside Daulatabad Fort or Deogiri Fort, Daulatabad, Maharashtra 00.jpg
images.caption:
After crossing the drawbridge over the moat, the only entrance to the interior of the fort is through a devious tunnel, which in times of siege was rendered impassable by an ingenious contrivance. The long ascending tunnel rises rapidly and tortuosly by a flight of steps, which are uneven in width and height, difficult for climb in the absence of light. The labyrinthine passage coupled with the darkness confuse the enemy army to kill themselves along a tunnel containing numerous chambers cut out of solid rock which were used in the olden times as guard rooms and store houses. The turns and twists lead to a window, now covered with grills, but was originally a trap set for enemy intruders, who on entering tumble down the slope to meet a watery grave in the moat below. The tunnel was impassable when the great obstacles come in the form of darkness, caltrops, barrier of smoke and a splash of hot oil or water from above. The steps in the courtyard are newly constructed for convenience of tourists.
Daulatabad Fort, originally Deogiri Fort, is a historic fortified citadel located in Daulatabad village near Aurangabad, Maharashtra, India. It was the capital of the Yadavas (9th century – 14th century CE), for a brief time the capital of the Delhi Sultanate (1327–1334), and later a secondary capital of the Ahmadnagar Sultanate (1499–1636).

Looking from southwest to northeast, the Nandi pavilion is photo left, with the south column to the right. Behind them the main bulk of the temple recedes east to the rear of the cliff.
